questions.title: A patient corrected with a minus 2 diopter cylinder axis 180 has:
questions.question: A patient corrected with a minus 2 diopter cylinder axis 180 has:

explanations.A: Simple hypermetropic astigmatism would need a plus, not minus, cylinder power; the sign here is minus, so this is myopic, not hypermetropic, astigmatism.
explanations.B: A prescription that is pure cylinder, with no sphere component, means only one meridian carries refractive error while the other is left at zero power (emmetropic) — this is by definition simple astigmatism. Because the cylinder power is minus, the affected meridian is myopic, making this simple myopic astigmatism. Had a sphere component also been present, or had both meridians been ametropic, it would be compound rather than simple.
explanations.C: Compound myopic astigmatism needs a spherical component alongside the cylinder (both meridians ametropic); a prescription with only a cylinder and no sphere is simple, not compound.
explanations.D: Simple myopia needs no cylindrical component at all (spherical error only); a cylinder-only prescription is astigmatism, not simple myopia.

questions.title: In keratoconus, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.question: In keratoconus, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Munson sign, a V-shaped indentation of the lower lid on downgaze from the cone-shaped cornea, is a genuine keratoconus sign, so it is true and not the exception being sought.
explanations.B: Corneal opacity (scarring) can occur in advanced keratoconus, particularly after acute hydrops, so this is true and not the exception being sought.
explanations.C: Corneal topography, showing an asymmetric, inferiorly steep pattern, is the key diagnostic test for keratoconus, so this is true and not the exception being sought.
explanations.D: The Kayser-Fleischer ring is a golden-brown ring of copper deposition in Descemet's membrane, a sign of Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), not of keratoconus. It has no association with corneal ectasia or thinning, so it does not belong among keratoconus's true features. Because this question asks which statement is NOT true, and the other three are genuine keratoconus facts, the Kayser-Fleischer ring is correctly the exception.

questions.title: Early senile nuclear cataract is accompanied by:
questions.question: Early senile nuclear cataract is accompanied by:

explanations.A: Early senile nuclear cataract increases the lens nucleus's refractive index as it sclerosis, producing a myopic (not hyperopic) shift of refraction — the classic "second sight" phenomenon where near vision transiently improves. This is one of the earliest detectable refractive changes in nuclear cataract, sometimes noticed before any visible opacity. It reverses as the cataract matures and vision progressively declines.
explanations.B: The refractive shift in early nuclear cataract is myopic, not hyperopic; the increased lens power shifts focus forward, not backward.
explanations.C: Night blindness is a retinal symptom (as in retinitis pigmentosa or vitamin A deficiency), not a feature of early nuclear cataract.
explanations.D: Cataract is characteristically painless; ocular pain suggests a different process, such as acute angle closure glaucoma or inflammation, not cataract itself.

questions.title: Which refractive error is characteristic of keratoconus?
questions.question: Which refractive error is characteristic of keratoconus?

explanations.A: Regular astigmatism has perpendicular principal meridians correctable by a spectacle cylinder; keratoconus instead produces irregular astigmatism.
explanations.B: Keratoconus shifts refraction toward myopia, not hypermetropia.
explanations.C: Keratoconus's asymmetric corneal steepening does not produce the regular, perpendicular-meridian astigmatism a spectacle cylinder can fully correct; instead it produces irregular astigmatism, whose surface is non-uniform, which is why rigid contact lenses often outperform spectacles. This irregular astigmatism, superimposed on progressive myopia, is the hallmark refractive picture of keratoconus. It is also why corneal topography, not keratometry alone, is needed to fully characterise it.
explanations.D: Emmetropia means no refractive error; keratoconus produces significant refractive error, not emmetropia.

questions.title: Hypermetropia means that the refractive system of the eye is:
questions.question: Hypermetropia means that the refractive system of the eye is:

options.D: The eye has long axial length.

explanations.A: Hypermetropia means the eye's overall refractive system is weaker than an emmetropic eye's, whether from a shorter axial length, flatter cornea, or weaker lens, so that parallel rays would focus behind the retina without extra convergence. This weaker system is why a hypermetropic eye must often accommodate even for distance vision. It is corrected by adding convergent power with a convex lens.
explanations.B: A refractive system stronger than the emmetrope's describes myopia, not hypermetropia.
explanations.C: A very steep cornea would make the eye's refractive system stronger, tending toward myopia, not the weaker system that defines hypermetropia.
explanations.D: Long axial length is a feature of myopia, not hypermetropia, which instead often has a short axial length.

questions.title: Presbyopia causes:
questions.question: Presbyopia causes:

explanations.A: Presbyopia affects near vision, not distance vision; difficulty seeing far suggests myopia or another distance refractive error, not presbyopia.
explanations.B: Presbyopia is the age-related weakening of accommodation that recedes the near point, making close tasks such as reading uncomfortable or blurred while distance vision, if otherwise emmetropic, remains unaffected. It typically becomes symptomatic from the mid-40s as the lens stiffens and ciliary efficiency declines. It is corrected with a convex reading addition, not a distance-vision change.
explanations.C: Unocular (monocular) diplopia is caused by conditions distorting one eye's optical path, such as lens subluxation or irregular astigmatism, not by presbyopia.
explanations.D: Subluxation of the crystalline lens is a structural zonular problem (for example, trauma or Marfan syndrome), unrelated to presbyopia's age-related accommodative decline.

questions.title: The simplest treatment of astigmatism is:
questions.question: The simplest treatment of astigmatism is:

explanations.A: Cycloplegia (paralysing accommodation with drops) is used to obtain an accurate refraction for diagnosis, not as a treatment for astigmatism itself.
explanations.B: Cylindrical lenses, whether in spectacles or as part of a sphero-cylindrical prescription, are the simplest, safest and most direct way to correct astigmatism, bending light differently along the two principal meridians to bring both into focus on the retina. They require no surgery and can be adjusted easily as the refractive error changes. Laser surgery and keratoplasty are reserved for cases where spectacle or contact lens correction is inadequate or undesired, not as first-line treatment.
explanations.C: Laser surgery (such as LASIK) can correct astigmatism but is a more invasive, non-simplest option compared with cylindrical lenses.
explanations.D: Keratoplasty (corneal transplantation) is a major surgical procedure reserved for corneal disease, far from the simplest astigmatism treatment.

questions.title: Keratoconus:
questions.question: Keratoconus:

options.C: Is best treated by eye drops.

explanations.A: Keratoconus is diagnosed by corneal topography, the Placido disc, retinoscopy and slit lamp, not primarily by ultrasound, which has no established diagnostic role here.
explanations.B: Keratoconus's asymmetric corneal thinning and steepening produces irregular, progressively increasing myopic astigmatism, so "can cause astigmatism" is a true statement about the disease. This astigmatism is often difficult to correct fully with spectacles because of its irregularity. It is one of the defining refractive consequences of the corneal ectasia.
explanations.C: Keratoconus is not treated with eye drops; management is contact lenses, collagen cross-linking or keratoplasty depending on severity.
explanations.D: Keratoconus is a progressive disease, not a static one; progression is exactly why cross-linking is offered to halt it.

questions.title: Keratoplasty means:
questions.question: Keratoplasty means:

options.B: Transplantation of a cornea from eye bank.
options.C: Excimer laser treatment of the cornea.

explanations.A: Intra-ocular lens implantation replaces the crystalline lens, typically after cataract surgery; it does not involve the cornea and is not keratoplasty.
explanations.B: Keratoplasty literally means transplanting corneal tissue, typically from an eye bank donor, to replace diseased or scarred host cornea, whether as a full-thickness (penetrating) or partial-thickness (lamellar) graft. It restores corneal clarity or shape when the patient's own cornea cannot be corrected by lenses or contact lenses alone. The depth of the recipient's disease dictates which specific keratoplasty type is used.
explanations.C: Excimer laser treatment of the cornea (as in LASIK or PRK) reshapes the patient's own corneal tissue; it does not transplant donor tissue and so is not keratoplasty.
explanations.D: Plastic surgery of the eyelids is blepharoplasty, an entirely different procedure on a different structure from keratoplasty.

questions.title: Mature intumescent cataract can be associated with:
questions.question: Mature intumescent cataract can be associated with:

explanations.A: An intumescent cataract typically causes significantly reduced visual acuity, not acuity better than 2/60; the swollen opaque lens blocks substantial light and image detail.
explanations.B: An intumescent cataract's swollen lens crowds the anterior segment, pushing the iris-lens diaphragm forward and shallowing the anterior chamber, which can precipitate secondary (phacomorphic) angle closure glaucoma with acutely raised intraocular pressure. This is a recognised, sight-threatening complication that makes prompt surgical removal important. Watching and waiting risks an acute pressure rise and permanent optic nerve damage.
explanations.C: A dense, swollen cataract blocks the fundus view, so the red reflex is dim, absent or glistening white, not "good."
explanations.D: Cataract, intumescent or otherwise, does not respond to medical treatment; surgical removal is required.

questions.title: The current treatment of cataract is:
questions.question: The current treatment of cataract is:

options.A: Intracapsular cataract surgery with IOL implantation.

explanations.A: Intracapsular cataract surgery, removing the whole lens with its capsule through a large incision, is an essentially obsolete technique, superseded by phacoemulsification.
explanations.B: Modern cataract surgery routinely implants an intraocular lens at the same sitting; phacoemulsification without lens implantation would leave the patient aphakic, which is not current standard practice.
explanations.C: The current standard of care for cataract surgery is phacoemulsification (ultrasonic emulsification and aspiration of the lens through a small incision) combined with implantation of an intraocular lens, restoring both clarity and refractive power in one procedure. This combination minimises incision size, promotes faster visual recovery and avoids the marked aphakic hypermetropia that would follow lens removal alone. It has replaced older, larger-incision techniques as routine practice.
explanations.D: Excimer laser corneal ablation reshapes the cornea for refractive error; it does not remove the cataractous lens and is not a cataract treatment.

questions.title: A Subluxated lens whether clear or cataractous:
questions.question: A Subluxated lens whether clear or cataractous:

options.D: It can be associated with other ocular or non-ocular manifestations.

explanations.A: Lens subluxation is not always unilateral; syndromic causes such as Marfan syndrome typically affect both eyes.
explanations.B: Lens subluxation can be strongly hereditary, as in Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria, both inherited conditions.
explanations.C: Treatment is not always conservative; surgical lens removal is indicated when subluxation causes significant visual impairment or complications such as glaucoma.
explanations.D: A subluxated lens, whether clear or cataractous, often signals an underlying systemic or syndromic cause — Marfan syndrome, homocystinuria, or trauma — each of which can carry its own further ocular or non-ocular manifestations. Recognising lens subluxation therefore prompts a broader systemic work-up, not just local ocular treatment. This associative pattern is a key reason subluxated lens is a clinically important sign beyond the eye itself.

questions.title: Myopic eye focuses images (With complete relaxation of accommodation):
questions.question: Myopic eye focuses images (With complete relaxation of accommodation):

explanations.A: Rays cannot meaningfully focus "in front of the lens" as a description of refractive error location; the relevant comparison is the image plane relative to the retina.
explanations.B: With accommodation fully relaxed, a myopic eye's excessive refractive power (or excessive axial length) brings parallel light rays to a focus in front of the retina rather than on it, producing blur for distance objects. This is the defining optical feature of myopia. Correction with a concave (diverging) lens pushes this focal point back onto the retina.
explanations.C: Focusing behind the retina describes hypermetropia (a weaker refractive system), not myopia.
explanations.D: "Behind the cornea" is not a meaningful description of where the myopic eye's image forms; the comparison is always to the retina.

questions.title: Hypermetropia can be corrected by:
questions.question: Hypermetropia can be corrected by:

explanations.A: Hypermetropia's weaker-than-emmetropic refractive system is corrected by adding convergent power with a convex (plus) lens, bringing the focal point forward onto the retina. This is the standard, general correction for hypermetropia at any age. It differs from a myopia correction, which instead diverges light with a concave lens.
explanations.B: A concave lens diverges light and is used to correct myopia, the opposite refractive error from hypermetropia.
explanations.C: A sphero-cylindrical lens is used when astigmatism coexists with a spherical error; it is not the general answer for pure hypermetropia correction.
explanations.D: A +2D lens for reading is a presbyopic addition for near work, not the general distance correction for hypermetropia.

questions.title: The current standard technique for cataract extraction in adults is:
questions.question: The current standard technique for cataract extraction in adults is:

options.B: Extracapsular cataract extraction with hard PMMA intraocular lens (IOL).
options.C: Removal of the lens matter by laser.
options.D: Phacoemulsification with posterior chamber foldable IOL.

explanations.A: LASIK reshapes the cornea for refractive error and does not remove the cataractous lens; it is not a cataract extraction technique.
explanations.B: Extracapsular cataract extraction with a rigid PMMA lens needs a much larger incision and has been superseded by phacoemulsification with a foldable lens as the current standard.
explanations.C: There is no standard technique that removes lens matter purely "by laser" without ultrasonic emulsification and aspiration; this does not describe current practice.
explanations.D: The current standard technique for adult cataract extraction is phacoemulsification combined with implantation of a foldable posterior-chamber intraocular lens, allowing the lens to be inserted through the same small, often sutureless incision used for phacoemulsification. This combination gives faster visual rehabilitation and lower complication rates than older large-incision techniques. It has become the routine approach in modern cataract surgery worldwide.

questions.title: A superficial corneal opacity is best treated by:
questions.question: A superficial corneal opacity is best treated by:

explanations.A: LASIK reshapes the cornea for refractive error correction; it does not address an existing opacity by replacing tissue.
explanations.B: Iridectomy creates an opening in the iris, typically for angle closure glaucoma prophylaxis; it is unrelated to corneal opacity treatment.
explanations.C: Phacoemulsification removes the crystalline lens for cataract; it does not treat corneal opacity.
explanations.D: A superficial corneal opacity, confined to the epithelium or anterior stroma, is best treated by lamellar keratoplasty, which replaces only the affected anterior corneal layers while preserving the healthy deeper stroma and endothelium. This selective approach avoids the risks of a full-thickness graft when the disease does not extend that deep. It also preserves more of the eye's own healthy tissue and endothelial cell reserve.

questions.title: Cataract typically presents as:
questions.question: Cataract typically presents as:

options.C: Slow progressive gradual diminution of vision.

explanations.A: Rapid diminution of vision is atypical for cataract and suggests another process (such as vascular occlusion or retinal detachment) unless a specific acute cause, such as trauma, is present.
explanations.B: A visual field defect is a sign of retinal or neuro-ophthalmic disease, not a typical cataract presentation, since cataract affects overall clarity rather than a discrete field area.
explanations.C: Cataract typically presents as a slow, progressive, gradual diminution of vision as the lens opacity accumulates over months to years, rather than a sudden visual loss. This gradual course, without pain, is one of its most characteristic clinical features. Any sudden vision change should prompt consideration of a different or additional diagnosis rather than uncomplicated cataract alone.
explanations.D: Limitation of ocular motility reflects extraocular muscle or orbital disease, not a lens opacity.

questions.title: Different Types of keratoplasties include the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Different Types of keratoplasties include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Penetrating keratoplasty (PKP), a full-thickness donor corneal graft, is a genuine keratoplasty type, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Deep lamellar keratoplasty, replacing stroma down to Descemet's membrane while retaining the host's own endothelium, is a genuine keratoplasty type, so it is not the exception.
explanations.C: Descemet's membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK), replacing only the diseased endothelium and Descemet's membrane, is a genuine keratoplasty type, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Application of intrastromal corneal ring segments reshapes a keratoconic cornea to improve its optics without transplanting any donor corneal tissue, so it is not itself a type of keratoplasty. Among the four options, it is the only one that does not involve grafting donor tissue, making it the correct exception. The other three are genuine transplantation techniques differing only by how much corneal tissue and which layers are replaced.

questions.title: Opacity of the crystalline lens is known as:
questions.question: Opacity of the crystalline lens is known as:

explanations.A: Leucoma is a dense white corneal scar, an opacity of the cornea, not the lens.
explanations.B: Opacity of the crystalline lens is, by definition, called cataract, distinguishing it from opacities or abnormalities of other ocular structures that can superficially resemble it. This terminology is fundamental to describing lens pathology accurately in clinical practice. Recognising the correct term avoids confusing lens disease with corneal, scleral or iris pathology.
explanations.C: Ciliary staphyloma is an abnormal bulging or ectasia of the sclera in the ciliary body region, unrelated to lens opacity.
explanations.D: Iris bombe is forward bowing of the iris from posterior synechiae blocking aqueous flow through the pupil; it does not describe lens opacity.

questions.title: A deep corneal opacity can be treated by:
questions.question: A deep corneal opacity can be treated by:

explanations.A: LASIK reshapes the patient's own cornea for refractive correction; it does not replace deep corneal tissue and cannot treat a deep opacity.
explanations.B: A deep corneal opacity extending through the full thickness of the stroma needs a full-thickness graft — penetrating keratoplasty — since a lamellar (partial-thickness) approach would leave residual opacity in the untouched deep layers. This depth-matching principle guides keratoplasty selection throughout corneal surgery. Penetrating keratoplasty replaces the entire thickness of the diseased cornea with a full-thickness donor button.
explanations.C: Iridectomy addresses the iris, not corneal opacity, and has no role in treating a deep corneal scar.
explanations.D: Phacoemulsification removes the crystalline lens; it does not address corneal tissue and cannot treat a deep corneal opacity.

questions.title: Complications of high myopia include the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Complications of high myopia include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Retinal detachment is a well-recognised complication of high myopia, from peripheral retinal thinning and vitreous traction, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.B: Macular hole is a recognised complication of high myopia, related to posterior globe stretching and vitreomacular traction, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.C: Corneal ulcer is an infective or inflammatory corneal surface process unrelated to the posterior-segment stretching that drives high myopia's complications, so it is not a recognised complication of high myopia. Among the four options, it is the one whose mechanism has nothing to do with globe elongation. The other three all follow directly from the stretched, thinned posterior globe characteristic of high myopia.
explanations.D: Choroidal neovascular membrane, following breaks in Bruch's membrane (lacquer cracks), is a recognised complication of high myopia, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.

questions.title: Regular astigmatism is characterized by:
questions.question: Regular astigmatism is characterized by:

options.A: The steep and flat axes are perpendicular.
options.B: The transition between the steep and flat meridian is acute.
options.C: Cannot be corrected by cylindrical lenses.

explanations.A: Regular astigmatism is defined by its two principal meridians, one steepest and one flattest, being perpendicular (90 degrees apart) to one another, with power changing smoothly between them. This perpendicular relationship and smooth power gradient is exactly what allows a single cylindrical lens, oriented along the correct axis, to fully correct it. Irregular astigmatism lacks this perpendicular, smooth pattern.
explanations.B: Regular astigmatism has a smooth, gradual transition in power between the steep and flat meridians, not an acute (abrupt) transition, which would instead suggest irregular astigmatism.
explanations.C: Regular astigmatism is, by definition, correctable by cylindrical lenses; this is one of its defining practical features, not something it lacks.
explanations.D: Regular astigmatism is not defined by an association with corneal opacities; it is a purely refractive, geometric description of the two principal meridians.

questions.title: One of the following surgeries is considered refractive surgery:
questions.question: One of the following surgeries is considered refractive surgery:

explanations.A: Trabeculectomy creates a new aqueous drainage pathway to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma; it does not correct refractive error.
explanations.B: Posterior capsulotomy (often with a YAG laser) clears a cloudy posterior lens capsule after cataract surgery; it does not correct refractive error.
explanations.C: Laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) reshapes the cornea to correct refractive error directly, making it a genuine refractive surgery. It is one of the standard surgical alternatives to spectacles or contact lenses for suitable candidates. Its effect is achieved by permanently altering corneal curvature with an excimer laser under a corneal flap.
explanations.D: Vitrectomy removes the vitreous, typically for retinal or vitreous disease; it does not correct refractive error.

questions.title: Regarding keratoconus, choose the WRONG answer:
questions.question: Regarding keratoconus, choose the WRONG answer:

options.A: It is conical thinning and protrusion of the cornea.
options.B: It causes progressively increasing myopia and myopic astigmatism.
options.C: It can be diagnosed by corneal topography.

explanations.A: Keratoconus is indeed conical thinning and protrusion of the cornea; this statement is correct, not the WRONG one being sought.
explanations.B: Keratoconus does cause progressively increasing myopia and myopic astigmatism; this statement is correct, not the WRONG one being sought.
explanations.C: Keratoconus is indeed diagnosed by corneal topography, its key diagnostic tool; this statement is correct, not the WRONG one being sought.

questions.title: Regarding facts about Cataract:
questions.question: Regarding facts about Cataract:

options.A: Mature cataract alone can cause no perception of light.
options.C: Complicated cataract can be caused by Astigmatism.

explanations.A: A mature cataract, even when dense, does not by itself cause complete no-perception-of-light vision; that suggests an additional posterior-segment or optic-nerve problem, not cataract alone.
explanations.B: An intumescent (swollen) cataract crowds the anterior chamber and can precipitate secondary (phacomorphic) angle closure glaucoma with an acute rise in intraocular pressure. This is a recognised, sight-threatening complication distinguishing intumescent cataract from an uncomplicated mature cataract. It is a key reason prompt surgical removal, rather than watchful waiting, is advised once intumescence is recognised.
explanations.C: Complicated cataract follows chronic intraocular inflammation (such as recurrent iritis or uveitis), not astigmatism, which is a purely refractive, not inflammatory, condition.
explanations.D: Cataract, whichever type, does not respond to medical treatment; surgical removal is required to restore vision.

questions.question: Symptoms of early senile nuclear cataract may include:

questions.title: The commonest cause of cataract is:
questions.question: The commonest cause of cataract is:

explanations.A: Trauma is a recognised but much less common cause of cataract than old age.
explanations.B: Diabetes is a recognised but much less common cause of cataract than old age, though it can accelerate cataract formation.
explanations.C: Hypoparathyroidism (via hypocalcaemia) is a rare, specific metabolic cause of cataract, far less common than age-related cataract.
explanations.D: Old age (senile cataract) is overwhelmingly the commonest cause of cataract worldwide, from cumulative oxidative and metabolic changes in the lens over decades. It far outpaces trauma, diabetes and endocrine/metabolic causes such as hypoparathyroidism in overall prevalence. This is why cataract surgery volumes rise steeply with an ageing population.

questions.title: Myopia is a condition which is:
questions.question: Myopia is a condition which is:

explanations.A: Myopia's excessive refractive power or long axial length focuses parallel rays in front of the retina, so correction needs a lens that diverges light before it enters the eye — a concave (minus) lens — to push the focal point back onto the retina. This is the standard, well-established correction for myopia. Concave lenses are recognisable on prescription by their negative (minus) sign.
explanations.B: A convex lens converges light and is the correction for hypermetropia, not myopia, which needs divergence instead.
explanations.C: In myopia, the image forms in front of, not behind, the retina; behind describes hypermetropia.
explanations.D: A myopic eye more often has a long, not small, axial length; a short eyeball is instead associated with hypermetropia.

questions.question: Band shaped keratopathy is commonly caused by deposition of:

explanations.D: Copper salt deposition describes the Kayser-Fleischer ring of Wilson's disease, not band keratopathy.

questions.title: Best option for management of anisometropia in unilateral aphakia:
questions.question: Best option for management of anisometropia in unilateral aphakia:

explanations.A: Spectacle correction of unilateral aphakia magnifies the aphakic eye's image by roughly 25-30%, producing anisokonia that is often poorly tolerated, making it a poor choice as the best option.
explanations.B: For unilateral aphakia, secondary intraocular lens implantation is the best management option, restoring the eye's optical power from within and avoiding the substantial image-size magnification (anisokonia) that spectacle correction produces, while giving more stable, permanent correction than a contact lens. This makes it the preferred definitive solution when feasible. It directly addresses the missing lens rather than compensating for its absence externally.
explanations.C: A contact lens is a reasonable non-surgical alternative, reducing anisokonia compared with spectacles, but intraocular lens implantation offers a more definitive, permanent solution and is considered the best option here.
explanations.D: Radial keratotomy is an older, largely obsolete refractive procedure for myopia; it has no role in correcting aphakia.

questions.question: Posterior dislocation of the lens is characterized by:

options.C: Neovascular glaucoma is a frequent complication

explanations.A: Posterior dislocation of the lens removes the lens's normal reflective surfaces from the visual axis, so the paired Purkinje-Sanson images (reflections from the anterior and posterior lens surfaces, normally used to assess lens position) are lost. explanations.C: Neovascular glaucoma is not a typical or frequent complication of posterior lens dislocation; angle closure or pupillary block glaucoma are more directly related mechanisms.
explanations.D: Posterior dislocation of the lens removes its refractive power from the visual axis, shifting the eye toward marked hypermetropia (aphakia-like), not myopia.

questions.question: Arcus senilis is characterized by:

options.A: It is formed of calcium deposits
options.B: It starts in the temporal and nasal corneal periphery and spreads circumferentially
options.C: It is formed of lipid deposits
options.D: It becomes indistinguishable from the limbus by the age of 60

explanations.A: Calcium deposits describe band keratopathy, not arcus senilis, which is caused by lipid deposition.
explanations.B: Arcus senilis classically begins superiorly and inferiorly before becoming circumferential, not starting in the temporal and nasal periphery as this option states.
explanations.C: Arcus senilis is a ring of lipid (cholesterol and phospholipid) deposition at the corneal periphery, a benign, extremely common age-related finding. Recognising lipid, not calcium, as the deposited material distinguishes it from band keratopathy, which is caused by calcium. Unlike band keratopathy, arcus senilis does not itself threaten vision and needs no treatment.
explanations.D: Arcus senilis remains a distinct peripheral ring rather than becoming indistinguishable from the limbus with age; this option does not correctly describe its natural history.

questions.title: Correction of unilateral aphakia with glasses will result in:
questions.question: Correction of unilateral aphakia with glasses will result in:

explanations.A: Astigmatism is not the specific consequence of spectacle-correcting unilateral aphakia; the defining problem is image-size mismatch (anisokonia), not induced astigmatism.
explanations.B: Glaucoma is not a direct consequence of the optical correction method chosen for aphakia; it is a separate potential complication of aphakia itself or its surgery.
explanations.C: The aphakic eye is already hypermetropic by nature of lacking a lens; spectacle correction addresses this refractive error rather than causing it, so hypermetropia is not the consequence of the correction method being asked about here.
explanations.D: Correcting unilateral aphakia with spectacles magnifies the aphakic eye's retinal image substantially, roughly 25-30% larger than the fellow phakic eye's image, producing anisokonia (unequal image size between the two eyes) that the brain often cannot fuse into single binocular vision. This is exactly why a contact lens or intraocular lens, both of which minimise this magnification difference, is preferred for unilateral aphakia. Anisokonia is the specific optical consequence spectacle correction of unilateral aphakia is known for.

questions.question: Astigmatism can be diagnosed with:

explanations.A: The Placido disc genuinely diagnoses astigmatism, but it is not the only correct tool among the options, since corneal topography and the astigmatic fan are also valid; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.B: Corneal topography genuinely diagnoses astigmatism, but it is not the only correct tool among the options, since the Placido disc and astigmatic fan are also valid; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.C: The astigmatic fan genuinely diagnoses astigmatism, but it is not the only correct tool among the options, since the Placido disc and corneal topography are also valid; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.D: Astigmatism can be diagnosed by several complementary tools: the Placido disc (projecting concentric rings distorted by an irregular or astigmatic cornea), corneal topography (a detailed map of corneal curvature), and the astigmatic fan (a subjective dial chart asking which spoke looks sharpest). Because all three genuinely detect and characterise astigmatism, "all of the above" is the correct, most complete answer. Using more than one method together often gives the most reliable overall assessment.

questions.title: Recession of the near point with ageing, making near vision uncomfortable, is termed:
questions.question: Recession of the near point with ageing, making near vision uncomfortable, is termed:

explanations.A: Recession of the near point with ageing, making near vision uncomfortable, is by definition presbyopia — the physiological, age-related decline in accommodative amplitude. This term specifically describes the near-point change itself, distinguishing it from other refractive or symptomatic terms. It typically becomes noticeable from the mid-40s onward.
explanations.B: Asthenopia describes eye strain or discomfort with use, a symptom that can accompany presbyopia (or other conditions), but it is not the specific term for near-point recession itself.
explanations.C: Hyperopia (hypermetropia) is a distance refractive error from a weak refractive system, a distinct condition from the age-related accommodative decline described here.
explanations.D: Since presbyopia is a genuine, specific and correct term for this description, "none of the above" is incorrect.

questions.question: Disadvantages of contact lenses include:

explanations.A: Infection risk is a genuine contact lens disadvantage, but it is not the only one among the options, since giant papillary conjunctivitis and traumatic abrasions are also genuine; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.B: Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a genuine contact lens disadvantage, but it is not the only one among the options, since infection risk and traumatic abrasions are also genuine; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.C: Traumatic corneal abrasions are a genuine contact lens disadvantage, but they are not the only one among the options, since infection risk and giant papillary conjunctivitis are also genuine; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.D: Contact lens wear carries several recognised disadvantages together: an increased risk of infection (from reduced corneal oxygenation and lens-surface biofilm), giant papillary conjunctivitis (a hypersensitivity reaction to lens deposits or edge), and traumatic corneal abrasions from insertion, removal or a poor fit. Because all three are genuine, well-documented risks, "all of the above" is the most complete and correct answer. This is why contact lens wearers need hygiene counselling and regular follow-up.

questions.question: Loss of accommodation may be found in:

explanations.A: Third nerve palsy genuinely causes lost accommodation, but it is not the only cause among the options, since presbyopia and cycloplegic drops also do; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.B: Presbyopia genuinely causes lost accommodation, but it is not the only cause among the options, since third nerve palsy and cycloplegic drops also do; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.C: Tropicamide eye drop instillation genuinely causes lost accommodation (cycloplegia), but it is not the only cause among the options, since third nerve palsy and presbyopia also do; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.

Because all three genuinely cause lost accommodation through different routes, "all of the above" is the correct, most complete answer. Recognising all three helps distinguish reversible from permanent causes.

questions.question: Retinal changes in myopes include all of the following except:

explanations.A: Temporal crescent (a peripapillary zone of exposed sclera or choroid from disc-margin stretching) is a genuine myopic fundus change, so it belongs among the true changes, not the exception.

questions.question: Myopia can be corrected by:

explanations.A: Myopia is corrected by concave (minus, diverging) lenses, which diverge incoming light before it enters the eye so the focal point moves back from in front of the retina onto it. questions.question: Keratoconus is diagnosed by:

questions.question: Diminution of vision in lens subluxation is caused by:

explanations.A: Myopia genuinely contributes to diminished vision in lens subluxation, but it is not the only mechanism among the options, since astigmatism and complications also contribute; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.B: Astigmatism genuinely contributes to diminished vision in lens subluxation, but it is not the only mechanism among the options, since myopia and complications also contribute; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.C: Complications (such as glaucoma, uveitis or cataract) genuinely contribute to diminished vision in lens subluxation, but they are not the only mechanism among the options, since myopia and astigmatism also contribute; "all of the above" is the more complete answer.
explanations.D: Diminution of vision in lens subluxation follows from several mechanisms together: induced myopia (from lens tilt or displacement altering effective power), induced astigmatism (from the tilted or decentred lens), and the subluxation's own complications such as glaucoma, uveitis or cataract. Because all three genuinely contribute to visual loss, "all of the above" is the correct, most complete answer. Recognising all three helps explain why lens subluxation's visual impact can be more complex than a simple refractive shift alone.

questions.title: On cycloplegic refraction, when one meridian is hyperopic and the other is myopic:
questions.question: On cycloplegic refraction, when one meridian is hyperopic and the other is myopic:

explanations.A: Simple astigmatism requires one meridian to be emmetropic (zero power) while only the other is ametropic; here both meridians are ametropic (one hyperopic, one myopic), so this is not simple astigmatism.
explanations.B: Compound astigmatism requires both meridians to be ametropic in the same direction (both hyperopic or both myopic); here one is hyperopic and the other myopic (opposite directions), so this is not compound astigmatism.
explanations.C: When cycloplegic refraction shows one principal meridian is hyperopic and the other is myopic, the two meridians are ametropic in opposite directions, which by definition is mixed astigmatism. This differs from simple astigmatism (one meridian emmetropic) and compound astigmatism (both meridians ametropic in the same direction). Recognising this pattern is important because mixed astigmatism's correction (a sphero-cylindrical lens straddling plano) differs from the other types.
explanations.D: Since mixed astigmatism is the correct, specific term for one hyperopic and one myopic meridian, "none of the above" is incorrect.

questions.title: Complications of hypermetropia include:
questions.question: Complications of hypermetropia include:

explanations.A: Hypermetropia's short axial length crowds the anterior segment, producing a shallow anterior chamber and narrow angle that predispose to angle closure glaucoma — this is hypermetropia's one well-established, hallmark complication among the five options. Recognising this link matters because it can precede any acute attack. It is the reason hypermetropic patients need periodic angle assessment as the anterior chamber tends to shallow further with age.
explanations.B: Iridocyclitis is not an established complication of hypermetropia; hypermetropia's recognised anterior-segment risk is specifically angle closure glaucoma from its crowded, shallow chamber.
explanations.C: Exotropia (divergent squint) is the wrong-direction association; uncorrected hypermetropia instead predisposes to convergent squint (accommodative esotropia) from excess accommodative convergence.
explanations.D: Choroidal neovascular membrane is a complication of high (pathological) myopia's stretched, elongated globe (through breaks in Bruch's membrane), not of hypermetropia's short, crowded globe.
explanations.E: Posterior staphyloma is likewise a complication of high (pathological) myopia's ectatic, thinned posterior globe wall, not of hypermetropia.

questions.title: Cylindrical lenses are prescribed for:
questions.question: Cylindrical lenses are prescribed for:

explanations.A: Myopia is corrected with a spherical concave lens, not specifically a cylindrical lens, unless astigmatism also coexists.
explanations.B: Hypermetropia is corrected with a spherical convex lens, not specifically a cylindrical lens, unless astigmatism also coexists.
explanations.C: Cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism specifically, bending light differently along the two principal meridians to bring both into focus on the retina, unlike a purely spherical lens which corrects the same power in every meridian. This is why cylindrical power is prescribed only when astigmatism is present, alongside any spherical correction needed. It is the standard, most direct correction for regular astigmatism.
explanations.D: Asthenopia (eye strain) is a symptom, not a refractive error corrected by a specific lens shape; treating its underlying cause, such as uncorrected refractive error, relieves it.
explanations.E: Cataract is a lens opacity treated surgically, not a refractive error corrected by any spectacle lens shape.

Examination revealed shallow anterior chamber with narrow angle.

options.C: This eye is predisposed to angle closure glaucoma.
options.D: Correction of this patient is with concave lens.

explanations.A: The patient's vision is 6/6 bilaterally without correction, arguing against significant myopia, which would typically blur uncorrected distance vision.
explanations.B: A shallow anterior chamber can accompany hypermetropia, but the vignette does not confirm a refractive diagnosis, and the specific, testable finding here is the angle closure glaucoma risk from the shallow chamber and narrow angle themselves.
explanations.C: The shallow anterior chamber and narrow angle found on examination directly predispose this eye to angle closure glaucoma, regardless of the exact refractive status, and are the specific abnormal sign this vignette highlights. Symptoms of headache and eye strain during close work in a patient with a crowded anterior segment should raise suspicion for this risk even before any acute attack occurs. Recognising a shallow chamber and narrow angle as an angle-closure risk factor is the key clinical point being tested.
explanations.D: A concave lens is the correction for myopia, not for a shallow-chamber, angle closure glaucoma-prone eye; prescribing a concave lens is not an appropriate response to this vignette's findings.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy presented with eye strain especially after reading. His mother noticed convergent squint especially on holding his mobile. Examination using cycloplegic revealed +5.0 sphere refraction both eyes. Visual acuity both eyes was 6/6.

options.A: In this child parallel rays come to focus behind the retina if he does not accommodate.
options.C: Treating the child with convex lens is essential.
options.D: Eye strain may be due to accommodative asthenopia.

explanations.A: It is true that, in hypermetropia, parallel rays focus behind the retina without accommodation, but this vignette's key answer identifies the necessary management step (convex-lens correction) as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.B: Uncorrected hypermetropia in a child drives convergent, not divergent, squint through excess accommodative convergence, so divergent squint would not be the expected finding.
explanations.C: This child's convergent squint, eye strain and +5.0 D hypermetropia together reflect excess accommodative convergence, so relieving the accommodative demand by correcting the underlying hypermetropia with a convex lens is the essential treatment step. Correcting the refractive error removes the need for the child to over-accommodate, treating the convergent squint and the asthenopia together at their common source. Left uncorrected, ongoing excess accommodation risks persistent squint and continued symptoms.
explanations.D: Eye strain from sustained excess accommodation is indeed a form of accommodative asthenopia, but this vignette's key answer identifies the necessary management step (convex-lens correction) as the specific point being tested here.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy presented with difficulty seeing the board in classroom. A year before he got same symptoms and eyeglasses were prescribed but he did not use them. His father was wearing myopic glasses.

options.A: In this boy parallel rays come to focus behind the retina with no accommodation.
options.B: In this boy parallel rays come to focus in front of the retina with no accommodation.
options.C: Convex lenses are used for treatment.
options.D: Sometimes this boy squeezes his eyes to get pin hole effect.

explanations.A: Parallel rays focusing behind the retina without accommodation describes hypermetropia, not this boy's myopic presentation.
explanations.B: A myopic eye's excessive refractive power (or long axial length) focuses parallel rays in front of, not behind, the retina when accommodation is fully relaxed, producing blur for distant objects such as the classroom board. This is the defining optical mechanism of this boy's presentation, especially given his father's own myopia suggesting a hereditary tendency. Recognising this focus point is fundamental to understanding why concave, not convex, correction is needed.
explanations.C: Myopia's excessive convergence needs a diverging concave lens to correct, not a convex lens, which would further increase convergence and worsen the blur.
explanations.D: Squeezing the eyes for a pinhole effect is a recognised behaviour in uncorrected myopic children, but this vignette's key answer identifies the underlying optical mechanism (rays focusing in front of the retina) as the specific point being tested here.

questions.title: A 22-year-old male came to ophthalmology clinic complaining of blurring of vision when looking at far objects although wearing his myopic glasses since he was 7 years old. questions.question: A 22-year-old male came to ophthalmology clinic complaining of blurring of vision when looking at far objects although wearing his myopic glasses since he was 7 years old. He said that the power of his glasses is increasing every year. His old glasses were -12.0 diopters bilaterally.

options.A: Your provisional diagnosis is pathological or degenerative myopia.
options.B: Short axial length of the globe is expected in this patient.
options.D: Open angle glaucoma is easy to diagnose in high myopic eyes.

explanations.A: A high, progressively increasing myopic correction (-12.0 D and rising) since childhood is the hallmark presentation of pathological (degenerative) myopia, distinguishing it from simple, stable myopia. This provisional diagnosis is the key clinical impression this vignette is building toward, given the progressive power increase over years. It sets up the expectation of the retinal and other complications that follow.
explanations.B: Pathological myopia is associated with a long, not short, axial length, as the globe progressively elongates.
explanations.C: Retinal complications may indeed occur in pathological myopia, but this vignette's key answer identifies the provisional diagnosis itself (pathological/degenerative myopia) as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.D: Open angle glaucoma coexisting with high myopia is notoriously difficult, not easy, to diagnose, since a myopic optic disc can itself look atypical and mimic or mask glaucomatous changes.

questions.question: A 45-year-old emmetropic female patient who never had to wear eyeglasses before, presented with inability to read small letters and blurred vision for near objects as sewing. Examination revealed vision for far is 6/6.

options.A: This condition is known as hypermetropia.
options.B: This is due to weakness of the ability to accommodate.
options.C: In this patient correction with concave lenses is advised.
options.D: This condition is known as presbyopia.

explanations.A: Hypermetropia is a distance refractive error from a weak refractive system; this patient's normal distance vision and isolated near-vision difficulty instead describe presbyopia, a different condition.
explanations.B: Weakness of the ability to accommodate is indeed the underlying mechanism of presbyopia, but this vignette's key answer identifies the correct name for the condition (presbyopia) as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.C: Presbyopia is corrected with convex reading lenses, not concave lenses, which would worsen near focus rather than help it.
explanations.D: This 45-year-old emmetropic patient's new difficulty reading small print and sewing, with preserved 6/6 distance vision, is the classic presentation of presbyopia — the age-related weakening of accommodation that recedes the near point while distance vision, if otherwise normal, is unaffected. Naming the condition correctly as presbyopia is the specific point this vignette tests. It typically appears in the mid-40s, matching this patient's age.

questions.title: A 68-year-old male came to outpatient clinic complaining of blurred vision in right eye and inability to see clearly. History of cataract operation right eye and IOL implantation 2 days before. Examination revealed corneal edema (increase in corneal thickness and haziness). Left cornea was clear.
questions.question: A 68-year-old male came to outpatient clinic complaining of blurred vision in right eye and inability to see clearly. History of cataract operation right eye and IOL implantation 2 days before. Examination revealed corneal edema (increase in corneal thickness and haziness). Left cornea was clear.

options.A: Corneal edema may be due to damage of endothelial cells of cornea.
options.B: Corneal edema in this patient may be due to herpetic eye disease.
options.C: Fuch's dystrophy is the cause of corneal edema in this patient.
options.D: Pumping of ions and fluids out of the cornea is mostly done by epithelial cells.

explanations.A: Corneal edema appearing just two days after cataract surgery and intraocular lens implantation is most likely due to mechanical damage of the corneal endothelial cells during surgery, which impairs their active ion-pumping function and lets the stroma swell with fluid. This is the most likely mechanism given the clear temporal link to recent intraocular surgery. Careful surgical technique and endothelial cell counts help predict and minimise this risk.
explanations.B: Herpetic eye disease can cause endotheliitis and corneal edema, but it is not suggested by this vignette's history of recent, otherwise uncomplicated cataract surgery, making surgical endothelial trauma the more likely explanation here.
explanations.C: Fuch's dystrophy is a chronic, progressive endothelial disease that would typically predate and complicate the surgery itself, rather than newly explain oedema appearing only two days postoperatively without prior mention.
explanations.D: The corneal endothelium, not the epithelium, is chiefly responsible for pumping ions and fluid out of the stroma to maintain corneal dehydration; the epithelium plays only a minor barrier role.

questions.title: A 34-year-old female came to outpatient clinic complaining of decreased vision in left eye. The patient also complained of foreign body sensation and lacrimation of same eye. Examination revealed entropion and lashes rubbing against cornea and corneal opacity. The patient stated she got before several attacks of red eye.
questions.question: A 34-year-old female came to outpatient clinic complaining of decreased vision in left eye. The patient also complained of foreign body sensation and lacrimation of same eye. Examination revealed entropion and lashes rubbing against cornea and corneal opacity. The patient stated she got before several attacks of red eye.

options.A: Trachoma may lead to corneal opacities through repeated trauma.
options.B: Disturbance of regular stromal collagen fibers is the cause of corneal opacity.
options.C: Regular collagen fibers cause scattering of light rays.
options.D: The cause of opacity in this patient is penetrating corneal trauma.

explanations.A: Trachoma scars the tarsal conjunctiva over repeated infective/inflammatory episodes, progressively distorting the lid margin into entropion with trichiasis (misdirected lashes); it is this repeated mechanical trauma from lash-corneal contact, cycle after cycle, that is trachoma's principal clinical route to corneal opacity in this vignette. This matches the entropion, lash-corneal rubbing and repeated red-eye history described. It is the specific clinical mechanism this question is testing.
explanations.B: Disturbance of regular stromal collagen fibre spacing is indeed the deeper tissue-level explanation for why trachoma's repeated trauma ultimately clouds the cornea, but this vignette's key answer identifies the clinical mechanism (repeated trauma from trichiasis/entropion) as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.C: Regular, evenly-spaced collagen fibres do not themselves scatter light — the opposite is true; it is the disturbance of that regularity that causes light scattering and opacity.
explanations.D: This patient's history of entropion, lash-corneal rubbing and repeated red-eye attacks describes chronic, repeated minor mechanical trauma from trichiasis, not a single episode of penetrating corneal trauma.

questions.title: A 62-year-old female patient presented complaining of a red, watery eye for the past two days with stitching pain and photophobia. Her vision has dropped to 6/24. She had history of diabetes for 10 years and was taking drops for dry eye but was otherwise healthy. Slit lamp examination revealed a corneal epithelial defect with positive fluorescein staining.
questions.question: A 62-year-old female patient presented complaining of a red, watery eye for the past two days with stitching pain and photophobia. Her vision has dropped to 6/24. She had history of diabetes for 10 years and was taking drops for dry eye but was otherwise healthy. Slit lamp examination revealed a corneal epithelial defect with positive fluorescein staining.

options.A: Diabetes may predispose to altering corneal epithelium and Bowman's membrane.
options.B: Stem cells are important for epithelial regeneration.
options.C: Chemical injuries never affect stem cells.
options.D: Decrease vision in this patient is due to endothelial cell loss.

explanations.A: Diabetes is a recognised predisposing factor for corneal epithelial vulnerability (diabetic keratopathy), altering the epithelium's basement-membrane adhesion and Bowman's membrane and impairing normal healing. This explains why this diabetic patient, already using dry-eye drops, developed a corneal epithelial defect with positive fluorescein staining and is at particular risk of slow or recurrent healing. Recognising diabetes as a predisposing factor for this kind of epitheliopathy is the specific point this vignette tests.
explanations.B: Limbal stem cells are indeed important for corneal epithelial regeneration generally, but this vignette's key answer identifies diabetes' predisposing effect on the epithelium and Bowman's membrane as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.C: Chemical injuries do affect limbal stem cells, contrary to this statement's claim that they "never" do; severe chemical burns are a well-recognised cause of stem cell damage and deficiency.
explanations.D: This vignette's pathology (a corneal epithelial defect with positive fluorescein staining) is an epithelial, not an endothelial, problem; endothelial cell loss would instead present with corneal oedema (increased thickness and haziness), not an epithelial staining defect.

questions.question: A 52-year-old female patient came to outpatient clinic complaining of gradual diminution of vision both eyes specially left eye. She said that she had severe dry eye with burning sensation and was diagnosed pemphigoid. Corneal opacities were detected.

options.A: A normal tear film is essential for corneal transparency.
options.B: Surface keratinization of cornea can occur in pemphigoid.
options.C: Prolonged and severe dry eyes never cause corneal opacities.
options.D: Decrease mucin layer of tears occurs in Sjogren's syndrome.

explanations.A: A normal tear film is indeed essential for corneal transparency, but this vignette's key answer identifies the specific consequence of pemphigoid (corneal keratinisation) as the point being tested here.
explanations.B: Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid is a chronic autoimmune blistering and scarring disease of the conjunctiva that, like trachoma, progressively destroys conjunctival goblet cells and scars the fornices; the resulting loss of the tear film's mucin layer leaves the ocular surface unable to wet normally, and over time the corneal epithelium can undergo surface keratinisation as a consequence. This matches this patient's severe dry eye, burning sensation, pemphigoid diagnosis and detected corneal opacities. Recognising keratinisation as a genuine consequence of pemphigoid is the specific point this vignette tests.
explanations.C: Prolonged, severe dry eye absolutely can cause corneal opacity, through mechanisms such as the surface keratinisation described here, so it does not "never" cause it, making this statement false.
explanations.D: Decreased mucin layer occurs through goblet cell loss in cicatricial disease such as pemphigoid and trachoma; Sjögren's syndrome instead chiefly reduces the aqueous (not mucin) layer via lacrimal gland destruction, so this statement misattributes the mechanism.

questions.question: A 30-year-old male patient came to ophthalmology clinic complaining of bilateral blurred vision. Examination revealed bilateral symmetrical corneal opacities. He stated that his father also had poor vision.

Identifying the affected layer therefore guides both prognosis and the choice of any surgical treatment.

questions.question: A 19-year-old male was complaining of frequent changing his glasses, his refraction was -7.0 sphere -5.0 cylinder. Central corneal linear striae were seen at posterior corneal stroma. Scissoring of red reflex on retinoscopy was detected.

options.A: Soft contact lenses are the main line of treating this condition.
options.B: The vertical striae are called Vogt striae.
options.C: Vernal conjunctivitis is a common association.
options.D: Down syndrome and Marfan syndrome are never an association.

explanations.A: Rigid, not soft, contact lenses are the main line of optical treatment for keratoconus, since they mask the irregular corneal surface far more effectively than a soft lens can.
explanations.B: The central corneal linear striae seen at the posterior stroma in this keratoconus patient, with scissoring of the red reflex on retinoscopy, are Vogt striae — fine vertical stress lines deep in the stroma that characteristically disappear with gentle pressure on the globe. Naming them correctly as Vogt striae is a key diagnostic recognition point in keratoconus. Their presence, alongside the scissoring reflex, supports the keratoconus diagnosis already suggested by this patient's frequently changing high astigmatic correction.
explanations.C: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis, not vernal conjunctivitis generically, is a recognised association of keratoconus through chronic eye rubbing, but this vignette's key answer identifies the correct name for the described corneal sign (Vogt striae) as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.D: Down syndrome and Marfan syndrome ARE recognised associations of keratoconus, not associations that "never" occur, making this statement false.

explanations.A: Refractive corneal surgery is not indicated during an acute hydrops episode; the priority is managing the acute oedema, not correcting refraction.
explanations.B: This patient's acute corneal oedema, with a fellow eye showing Munson sign in a known keratoconus patient, describes acute hydrops — sudden stromal oedema following a break in Descemet's membrane from excessive stretching over the progressively thinning, ectatic cornea. Examination revealed clear cornea. The red reflex showed black sectors and vision of right eye was 5/60 and 6/18 left eye.

options.A: The patient may have immature senile cataract.
options.B: Most common cause of cataract is congenital cataract.

explanations.B: Congenital cataract is a much rarer, paediatric-onset condition; old age remains the overwhelmingly commonest cause of cataract in an elderly patient like this one.
explanations.C: A mature cataract would show an absent, not partially preserved black-sectored, red reflex; this patient's findings instead describe an immature cataract.
explanations.D: Uveitis is not supported by this vignette's history, which lacks any inflammatory signs or symptoms; a straightforward age-related cataract is the more consistent explanation.

The patient gave no history of local or systemic disease. Examination revealed vision was hand movement in left eye compared to 4/60 right eye. The left red reflex appeared white. The left capsule was glistening, and the anterior chamber was shallow.

options.A: The most probable diagnosis is left nuclear cataract.
options.B: The most probable diagnosis is left intumescent cataract.
options.C: The IOP intraocular pressure may become acutely elevated.
options.D: Cataract surgery may be postponed for one year.

explanations.A: A nuclear cataract does not typically present with a glistening, swollen anterior capsule and markedly shallow anterior chamber; those features specifically describe an intumescent cataract instead.
explanations.B: This patient's glistening white anterior capsule and shallow anterior chamber, alongside a white red reflex and hand-movement vision, describe an intumescent cataract — a swollen lens pushing the iris-lens diaphragm forward. This is distinct from a simple nuclear cataract, which would not typically show this glistening, swollen appearance or such a markedly shallow chamber. Recognising the intumescent pattern is important because of its associated glaucoma risk.
explanations.C: Acutely elevated intraocular pressure is indeed a genuine risk with an intumescent cataract, but this vignette's key answer identifies the diagnosis itself (intumescent cataract) as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.D: Cataract surgery should not be postponed when an intumescent cataract is recognised, given its acute angle closure glaucoma risk; prompt removal is advised instead.

options.B: Most probable diagnosis is lens subluxation.

explanations.A: Posterior dislocation would remove the lens entirely from the pupillary axis into the vitreous, unlike this vignette's finding of the lens edge still visible across the pupil, which instead describes subluxation.
explanations.B: This patient's monocular diplopia with the lens edge visible across the pupil, following blunt trauma, describes lens subluxation — partial zonular rupture displacing but not fully dislocating the lens — rather than complete dislocation, since part of the lens remains within the pupillary axis. The irregular anterior chamber depth further supports a lens that has shifted position but not fully separated from its zonular support.
explanations.C: Astigmatism may indeed be present with lens subluxation from the tilted lens, but this vignette's key answer identifies the diagnosis itself (lens subluxation) as the specific point being tested here.
explanations.D: Marfan syndrome is indeed a recognised association of lens subluxation, but this vignette's key answer identifies the diagnosis itself (lens subluxation) as the specific point being tested here, separate from any syndromic cause (this case being traumatic).

questions.question: In simple myopic astigmatism, the prescribed spectacles are:

explanations.A: A convex spherical lens would be entirely the wrong shape (spherical, not cylindrical, needed for astigmatism) and the wrong sign (convex/plus, when a myopic meridian needs minus power).
explanations.B: A concave spherical lens has the correct sign (minus, for the myopic meridian) but the wrong shape; a purely spherical lens cannot correct the astigmatic (cylindrical) component of this error.
explanations.C: Simple myopic astigmatism has one meridian myopic and the other emmetropic, so correction needs only a cylindrical (not spherical) lens, and because the ametropic meridian is myopic, the cylinder power must be minus (concave), diverging light in that meridian to bring it into focus on the retina. This combination, concave and cylindrical, precisely matches both the type and direction of this refractive error. Getting either the shape or the sign wrong would fail to correct this specific error.
explanations.D: A convex cylindrical lens has the correct shape (cylindrical, for astigmatism) but the wrong sign; a myopic meridian needs minus (concave), not plus (convex), power.

explanations.A: Accommodation is entirely lost, not in excess, in aphakia, since the lens whose shape change produces accommodation is absent.

questions.title: In accommodation:
questions.question: In accommodation:

options.A: The refractive power of the eye decreases.

explanations.A: During accommodation, the eye's refractive power increases, not decreases, as the lens rounds up and gains converging power for near focus.
explanations.B: During accommodation, the ciliary muscle contracts, not relaxes, which slackens the zonules and allows the elastic lens to round up.
explanations.C: Accommodation is driven by increased parasympathetic, not sympathetic, tone to the ciliary muscle.
explanations.D: Accommodative amplitude physiologically declines with age, as the lens stiffens and loses elasticity and the ciliary muscle's efficiency reduces, culminating in presbyopia by the mid-40s. This age-related decline is a normal, universal process, not a disease. It is the basis for why virtually everyone eventually needs a reading correction regardless of their distance refractive status.

questions.title: Corneal dehydration is a responsibility of:
questions.question: Corneal dehydration is a responsibility of:

explanations.A: The corneal epithelium contributes only a minor barrier role to limiting fluid entry; it is not primarily responsible for actively pumping fluid out of the stroma.
explanations.B: The stroma is the tissue being kept relatively dehydrated by the endothelial pump; it is not itself the pumping structure.
explanations.C: Corneal dehydration (relative deturgescence), essential for corneal transparency, is the responsibility of the corneal endothelium's active Na+/K+-ATPase ion pumps, which continuously pump fluid and ions out of the stroma against its natural tendency to imbibe water. This active pumping is what keeps the stroma from swelling and clouding. Damage to the endothelium, from surgery, disease or trauma, directly impairs this dehydrating function and produces corneal oedema.
explanations.D: Bowman's membrane is an acellular structural layer beneath the epithelium with no active pumping function; it plays no role in corneal dehydration.

questions.title: One of the clinical signs that is characteristic to keratoconus is:
questions.question: One of the clinical signs that is characteristic to keratoconus is:

explanations.A: Haab's striae are horizontal breaks in Descemet's membrane from congenital glaucoma's stretched cornea, not a keratoconus sign.
explanations.B: Vogt striae — fine, vertical stress lines deep in the corneal stroma that disappear with gentle pressure on the globe — are among the most characteristic clinical signs of keratoconus, reflecting the mechanical stress of progressive corneal thinning and protrusion. Their presence on slit-lamp examination is a classic bedside confirmation of the diagnosis. They are frequently tested alongside Munson sign as keratoconus's signature external and slit-lamp findings.
explanations.C: "Corneal double stain" is not a recognised keratoconus sign.
explanations.D: Herbert's pits are shallow limbal follicle scars characteristic of trachoma, not a keratoconus sign.

questions.title: The most expected refraction in a case of keratoconus is:
questions.question: The most expected refraction in a case of keratoconus is:

explanations.A: Keratoconus shifts refraction toward myopia, not hypermetropia, so high hypermetropia is not the expected pattern.
explanations.B: High myopia alone is incomplete; keratoconus's astigmatism, from the irregular corneal surface, is an equally characteristic and expected component of its refractive picture.
explanations.C: While the astigmatism in keratoconus is often irregular, "against the rule" specifically describes a regular-astigmatism axis orientation, not the specific, most expected keratoconus pattern of myopic astigmatism.
explanations.D: As keratoconus's cone-shaped cornea steepens irregularly, refraction shifts toward progressively increasing myopia combined with irregular astigmatism — myopic astigmatism is therefore the most expected refractive pattern in this disease. This combination, rather than either myopia or astigmatism alone, is what distinguishes keratoconus's refractive signature. It is also why spectacle correction often underperforms compared with rigid contact lenses, which better mask the irregular astigmatic component.

questions.title: In posterior dislocation, the pupil is:
questions.question: In posterior dislocation, the pupil is:

explanations.A: When the lens dislocates fully posteriorly into the vitreous, the pupil, no longer partially filled by the lens, appears uniformly and strikingly dark on examination — described as a "jet black pupil" — since no lens surface remains centrally to produce the usual red-reflex or Purkinje-Sanson reflections. This distinctive appearance is a specific bedside clue to posterior lens dislocation. It reflects the same underlying loss of central lens tissue that also explains the deepened anterior chamber and lost Purkinje-Sanson images in this condition.
explanations.B: A "peaked" pupil describes a different distortion, such as from iris incarceration in a wound, not the specific appearance of posterior lens dislocation.
explanations.C: A festooned pupil describes irregular scalloping typically from posterior synechiae or a partially subluxated lens edge, not the specific jet-black appearance of full posterior dislocation.
explanations.D: "Irregular" is too vague to capture the specific, distinctive jet-black pupil appearance that posterior lens dislocation classically produces.

questions.title: Severe lens subluxation may cause:
questions.question: Severe lens subluxation may cause:

explanations.A: Binocular diplopia arises from misalignment between the two eyes (such as a squint), not from a single eye's optical pathway, so it is not the type of diplopia lens subluxation produces.
explanations.B: Severe lens subluxation displaces the lens enough that part of the pupil's visual field passes through the lens while another part passes around its edge (the aphakic portion), producing two overlapping images from the same eye — monocular, not binocular, diplopia. This diplopia persists even when the fellow eye is covered, distinguishing it from a binocular alignment problem. It is one of the more specific symptoms prompting suspicion of lens subluxation.
explanations.C: Myopic shift can occur with lens subluxation from altered effective lens power, but this item's key answer identifies monocular diplopia as the specific consequence being tested here.
explanations.D: Anisokonia is an image-size difference between the two eyes, typically from unequal refractive correction (such as unilateral aphakia), not the specific symptom of severe unilateral lens subluxation being tested here.

questions.title: Commonest causes of vitreous hemorrhage are the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Commonest causes of vitreous hemorrhage are the following EXCEPT:

options.D: Posterior vitreous detachment causing retinal tear.

explanations.A: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy's fragile new vessel rupture is the commonest overall cause of vitreous haemorrhage, so it belongs among the true commonest causes, not the exception.
explanations.B: Trauma is a well-recognised commonest cause of vitreous haemorrhage, so it belongs among the true commonest causes, not the exception.
explanations.C: Uveitis (intraocular inflammation) is not among the established commonest causes of vitreous haemorrhage; while severe inflammatory disease can occasionally contribute to bleeding, it does not rank among the leading, well-established mechanisms. Among the four options, it is therefore the one that is NOT a commonest cause, which is exactly what this EXCEPT-format question asks for. The other three are all recognised as the leading causes of vitreous haemorrhage in clinical practice.
explanations.D: Posterior vitreous detachment causing a retinal tear is a well-recognised commonest cause of vitreous haemorrhage, so it belongs among the true commonest causes, not the exception.

questions.title: Complications of anterior lens dislocation include the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Complications of anterior lens dislocation include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Anterior lens dislocation does not itself breach the cornea; corneal perforation, a full-thickness corneal defect, is not a mechanism this condition produces without an accompanying penetrating injury. Among the four options, it is therefore the one that is NOT a recognised complication of anterior lens dislocation, which is exactly what this EXCEPT-format question asks for. The other three all follow directly from the dislocated lens's presence in or near the anterior chamber angle and iris.
explanations.B: Glaucoma, from angle obstruction by the anteriorly dislocated lens, is a genuine complication of anterior lens dislocation, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.C: Iridocyclitis, from mechanical irritation of the iris and ciliary body by the dislocated lens, is a genuine complication of anterior lens dislocation, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.D: Cataract, from disrupted lens metabolism after dislocation, is a genuine complication of anterior lens dislocation, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.

questions.title: Lens subluxation:
questions.question: Lens subluxation:

options.A: Patient may complain of binocular diplopia.
options.B: There is loss of Purkinje-Sanson images.

explanations.A: Lens subluxation, when it causes diplopia, produces monocular, not binocular, diplopia, since the effect arises within a single eye's optical pathway.
explanations.B: Lens subluxation displaces the lens's reflective anterior and posterior surfaces from their normal position, disrupting the paired Purkinje-Sanson images that these surfaces normally produce. This loss is a specific, examinable sign that helps confirm lens malposition on clinical examination. It reflects the same underlying mechanism seen in full lens dislocation, just to a lesser degree.
explanations.C: Surgery is not the only treatment for lens subluxation; mild, stable subluxation without significant visual impairment or complications can be observed rather than operated on.
explanations.D: Astigmatism is not always present with lens subluxation; its presence depends on the degree and direction of lens tilt or decentration, which varies case to case.

questions.title: Subluxated lens is found in all the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Subluxated lens is found in all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Marfan syndrome, through connective-tissue zonular weakness, is a well-recognised cause of lens subluxation, so it belongs among the true associations, not the exception.
explanations.B: Homocystinuria, through a distinct zonular-fibre defect, is a well-recognised cause of lens subluxation, so it belongs among the true associations, not the exception.
explanations.C: Trauma is a well-recognised cause of lens subluxation through direct zonular rupture, so it belongs among the true associations, not the exception.
explanations.D: Behcet's disease is a systemic vasculitis whose recognised ocular association is recurrent uveitis, not zonular weakness or lens subluxation. Among the four options, it is therefore the one that is NOT a recognised cause of subluxated lens, which is exactly what this EXCEPT-format question asks for. The other three are all well-established causes or associations of lens subluxation.

questions.title: The following test is done to determine visual prognosis after surgery:
questions.question: The following test is done to determine visual prognosis after surgery:

explanations.A: When a dense cataract or other media opacity prevents formal visual acuity or fundus examination, projection of light — testing whether the patient can correctly identify the direction a light is shone from — estimates whether the retina and optic nerve behind the opacity are still functioning well enough to justify surgery. Accurate directional projection implies grossly intact posterior visual pathway function despite the opaque view. This makes it the standard, practical test for visual prognosis before surgery in such an eye.
explanations.B: Fluorescein angiography images retinal and choroidal blood vessels; it needs a clear enough view of the fundus and does not serve as a general pre-operative visual-prognosis test through a dense opacity.
explanations.C: Formal visual field testing needs a clear enough media and reliable fixation, both of which a dense opacity compromises, making it impractical for this specific pre-operative purpose.
explanations.D: Corneal topography assesses corneal shape, unrelated to retinal or optic nerve function, and so does not serve to estimate visual prognosis through a lens opacity.
